section.title: Judgment and a Promise of Restoration
section.sectionRationale: The vision that began with idolatry in the temple now turns to the wicked counselors who plot violence in Jerusalem, and to the exiles the city despises as cast off. In the middle of this scene of judgment, right where hope seems impossible, God speaks His clearest promise yet: a new heart, a new spirit, and a gathering home, before the glory finally lifts off the city altogether.
section.thesis: God judges Jerusalem's wicked leaders and their false confidence that the exiles are 'far from the LORD', yet in the same breath He promises the very exiles they despise a new heart and a new spirit, proving that His discipline always serves His larger purpose of restoration, a purpose brought to completion in the new covenant secured by Christ.
section.frameNote: Three movements: judgment on the wicked counselors who treat Jerusalem as a cooking pot and its people as meat, ending in Pelatiah's sudden death; the promise to the scattered exiles of gathering, a new heart, and a new spirit; and the glory's final rise from the city to the mountain on its east side.

verses.text: Then the Spirit lifted me up and brought me to the gate of the house of the LORD that faces east. And there at the entrance of the gate were twenty-five men. Among them I saw Jaazaniah son of Azzur and Pelatiah son of Benaiah, who were leaders of the people.
And the LORD said to me, “Son of man, these are the men who plot evil and give wicked counsel in this city.
They are saying, ‘Is not the time near to build houses? The city is the cooking pot, and we are the meat.’
Therefore prophesy against them; prophesy, O son of man!”
And the Spirit of the LORD fell upon me and told me to declare that this is what the LORD says: “That is what you are thinking, O house of Israel; and I know the thoughts that arise in your minds.
You have multiplied those you killed in this city and filled its streets with the dead.
Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: The slain you have laid within this city are the meat, and the city is the pot; but I will remove you from it.
You fear the sword, so I will bring the sword against you, declares the Lord GOD.
I will bring you out of the city and deliver you into the hands of foreigners, and I will execute judgments against you.
You will fall by the sword, and I will judge you even to the borders of Israel. Then you will know that I am the LORD.
The city will not be a pot for you, nor will you be the meat within it. I will judge you even to the borders of Israel.
Then you will know that I am the LORD. For you have neither followed My statutes nor practiced My ordinances, but you have conformed to the ordinances of the nations around you.”
Now as I was prophesying, Pelatiah son of Benaiah died. Then I fell facedown and cried out in a loud voice, “Oh, Lord GOD, will You bring the remnant of Israel to a complete end?”

units.label: A new heart and a new spirit
units.note: gathering, cleansing, and transformation promised to the exiles

verses.text: Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying,

“Son of man, your brothers, your relatives, your fellow exiles, and the whole house of Israel, are those of whom the people of Jerusalem have said, ‘They are far away from the LORD; this land has been given to us as a possession.’

Therefore declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Although I sent them far away among the nations and scattered them among the countries, yet for a little while I have been a {{miqdash_meat|sanctuary}} for them in the countries to which they have gone.’

Therefore declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘I will gather you from the peoples and assemble you from the countries to which you have been scattered, and I will give back to you the land of Israel.’
When they return to it, they will remove all its detestable things and all its abominations.
And I will give them {{lev_echad|singleness of heart}} and put a {{ruach_chadashah|new spirit}} within them; I will remove their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh,
so that they may follow My statutes, keep My ordinances, and practice them. Then they will be My people, and I will be their God.
But as for those whose hearts pursue detestable things and abominations, I will bring their conduct down upon their own heads, declares the Lord GOD.”

units.label: The glory rises from the city
units.note: to the mountain on the east

verses.text: Then the cherubim, with the wheels beside them, spread their wings, and the glory of the God of Israel was above them.
And the glory of the LORD rose up from within the city and stood over the mountain east of the city.
And the Spirit lifted me up and carried me back to Chaldea, to the exiles in the vision given by the Spirit of God. After the vision had gone up from me,
I told the exiles everything the LORD had shown me.

miqdash_meat.gloss: A sanctuary in small measure, or a little sanctuary. Even in exile, far from the ruined temple, God graciously makes Himself present with His scattered people in a lesser but real way, a foretaste of His presence not being confined to one building or land.

lev_echad.gloss: One heart, or singleness of heart. Where the people's hearts were divided between the LORD and idols, God promises to unify their affection and loyalty entirely toward Himself.

ruach_chadashah.gloss: A new spirit. Paired with the removal of a heart of stone and the gift of a heart of flesh, this promise anticipates the New Testament gift of the Holy Spirit who enables obedience from within rather than mere external conformity.

basic.context: Ezekiel is shown the very leaders who plot violence in Jerusalem and dismiss the exiles as cut off from the LORD. God judges those leaders, yet turns immediately to comfort the exiles with an astonishing promise: a new heart and a new spirit, so that they will finally, truly, obey Him. Only after this promise does the glory finally lift off the city and move east.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real vision given to Ezekiel among the exiles, addressing an actual dispute over who truly belonged to God, those left in Jerusalem or those already deported. The hardest, most needed lesson is that outward proximity to the temple, or geography, or ancestry, does not guarantee closeness to God; genuine transformation of heart does.
basic.originalLanguages: God calls Himself a miqdash me'at, a little sanctuary, to the scattered exiles, showing His presence is not chained to one building. He then promises lev echad, one heart, and ruach chadashah, a new spirit, replacing a heart of stone with a heart of flesh, the clearest Old Testament anticipation of the inward transformation the New Testament calls the new birth.
basic.typology: The promised new heart and new spirit anticipate the new covenant of Jeremiah 31:31-34 and its fulfillment in the gift of the Holy Spirit, who now writes God's law on believers' hearts, 2 Corinthians 3:3, Hebrews 8:10, enabling from within the obedience the old covenant could only command from outside.
basic.christ: Jesus is the mediator of the new covenant Ezekiel here anticipates, Luke 22:20, Hebrews 8:6-13; through His Spirit, poured out at Pentecost, He accomplishes exactly what Ezekiel 11:19-20 promises, replacing hearts of stone with hearts responsive to God, so that His people can at last keep His statutes, not by their own effort but by His indwelling Spirit.
basic.god: God is just, holding wicked leaders accountable for the violence and false confidence that fills the city; yet He is also tenderly gracious to the very people the city despises, promising the exiles a sanctuary in exile, a homecoming, and a transformed heart, proving His judgment and His mercy flow from the same covenant faithfulness.
basic.crossReferences: Jeremiah 31:31-34 promises the new covenant written on the heart. 2 Corinthians 3:3 and Hebrews 8:10 apply this promise directly to believers in Christ. Ezekiel 36:26-27 repeats and expands this same new heart and new spirit promise. Acts 2 records the Spirit's outpouring that begins its fulfillment.
basic.oneStory: This is the moment judgment and hope meet in the same breath: God judges the proud counselors of a doomed city, yet promises the despised exiles a heart transplant that no circumstance can undo. Every page after this runs toward the day that promise is kept fully in Christ, who gives His Spirit so that God's people at last love and obey Him from the heart.

context.literary:
Chapter 11 closes the long vision of 8:1 to 11:25 and has three movements, each opened by a fresh signal. First, the Spirit lifts Ezekiel to the east gate, and he faces twenty-five men and two named leaders, 11:1 to 13. Then a new word of the LORD comes, 11:14, and the scene turns from the city to the exiles, 11:14 to 21. Finally the vision itself resumes, with the cherubim and the glory, and ends with Ezekiel carried back to Chaldea, 11:22 to 25. A judgment, a promise and a departure, in that order, and the promise sits exactly at the center.

The first movement is a controlled reversal of a slogan. The men say the city is the pot and they are the meat, 11:3, meaning that the walls will keep them safe. God turns the picture inside out: the slain they have heaped up are the meat, the city is the pot, and the men themselves will be taken out of it, 11:7 and 11:11. The same Hebrew words will be heard again at 11:19, where the word for meat, basar, becomes the word for the heart of flesh God will give. What the elite imagined as their safety is replaced by what God offers as His cure.

The chapter also answers chapter 9 in a deliberate way. In 9:8 Ezekiel cried out that God would destroy the whole remnant, and the answer was a stern defence of the judgment. In 11:13, after Pelatiah dies, he asks nearly the same question, and this time the answer is a promise. Both movements close with the same verdict on the stubborn, that God will bring their conduct down on their own heads, 9:10 and 11:21. The hope in the middle has a hard edge on either side.
context.historical:
Ezekiel speaks from exile in 592 BC or so, five years after the first deportation of 597, 2 Kings 24:14 to 16. The Jerusalem leaders had stayed behind, and the people who were left reasoned from the facts. The ones who were taken had been the stronger, the craftsmen, the princes and the king, and yet they were now in Babylon. Those who remained took this to be a sign of favour. The slogan of 11:15 is a good example: the exiles are far from the LORD, and the land has been given to us. A later version of the same thinking, after the city fell, was spoken by survivors among the ruins who said that Abraham was one man and had the land, while they were many, Ezekiel 33:24.

Jeremiah, writing to the exiles from Jerusalem, gave the opposite assessment. In his vision of two baskets, the exiles were the good figs and those who remained were the bad ones, Jeremiah 24:5 to 8. He also wrote to the exiles to build houses and settle down, Jeremiah 29:5 to 7, which makes the leaders' phrase about building houses in 11:3 sound like a deliberate mockery of that letter or a competing slogan to it. Ezekiel and Jeremiah agree: the safe place is not the city but the people who are scattered with God.

The judgments in 11:8 to 11 were remembered in what came next. Leading men of Jerusalem were brought to the king of Babylon at Riblah, in the land of Hamath, near the far northern edge of Israel's territory, and put to death there, 2 Kings 25:20 and 21. Readers have long heard in this the fulfilment of the promise that they would be judged 'to the borders of Israel,' Ezekiel 11:10 and 11:11. Pelatiah's death in 11:13 is the one detail that the vision shares with real time: it happened while Ezekiel was prophesying, in the sight of the exiles who would later be told.
context.canonical:
The chapter is one of the most densely connected in the prophets. Its promise of a new heart is echoed in Ezekiel 36:24 to 28, with a longer treatment that adds cleansing water and the gift of God's own Spirit, and in 37:14, 'I will put My Spirit in you and you will live.' Jeremiah has the same promise as a new covenant, with the law written on the heart, Jeremiah 31:31 to 33, and as 'one heart and one way,' Jeremiah 32:39. Behind all of them lies Moses' promise that the LORD Himself would circumcise the hearts of the people so that they might love Him, Deuteronomy 30:6, and the prayer of David, 'Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me,' Psalm 51:10.

The New Testament treats the promise as fulfilled in Christ. Jesus takes the cup as 'the new covenant in My blood,' Luke 22:20. Paul tells the Corinthians that they are a letter from Christ written 'not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts,' 2 Corinthians 3:3, and Hebrews quotes Jeremiah in full to say that the new covenant has come, Hebrews 8:8 to 12. Jesus' conversation with Nicodemus, in which being born of water and the Spirit is said to be a requirement for the kingdom, John 3:3 to 10, rests on the same promises, and Jesus is surprised that a teacher of Israel does not know them.

The last verses of the chapter, with the glory resting on the mountain east of the city, find an echo in the Mount of Olives, from which Jesus ascended, Acts 1:9 to 12, and on which His feet will stand, Zechariah 14:4.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The prophet speaks to two audiences and means to unsettle both. For the leaders in Jerusalem, the word is that their confidence is a lie. They plot evil, they rely on walls, and they are tormented by a fear of the sword that they will not turn from. For the exiles, the word is that they are not the forgotten. They have been taken to be far from God, and the LORD says that He Himself has been their sanctuary where they are. These two messages are one message: God is where He chooses to be, and He is not where the powerful say He is.

Ezekiel also wants the exiles to hear that their situation is not the end of the story. The promise of 11:17 to 20 has four verbs of gathering and giving: gather, assemble, give back the land, give a new heart. The order matters. The people are not told that the return depends on a prior reform of their hearts, only that when they return they will remove all the detestable things, 11:18, and that God will make that obedience possible. For a people crushed by the weight of their own failure, the real news is that God is going to do in them what they cannot do themselves.

The chapter ends with the glory leaving and the prophet being carried back to tell what he has seen. He is not told to keep quiet. He is told, in effect, to carry the whole of it, the verdict and the hope together, and the last verse says that he told the exiles everything the LORD had shown him.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This chapter records a conflict between two groups of Judeans and the word God spoke over both. It is not a general rule that those who are far from the centre of religious life are the favoured ones, nor that those who hold the institutions are always the guilty. The principle is narrower: God judges those who use religious position and civil security to excuse violence and idolatry, and He keeps faith with those who have lost the visible signs of belonging.

The promise of a new heart is addressed to the exiles, and the New Testament teaches that it has been fulfilled in the church by the Spirit, 2 Corinthians 3:3 and Hebrews 8:10. That means the passage describes what God promised to do, and it is not a command to produce a new heart by effort. The commands to repent in the book, such as Ezekiel 18:31, 'fashion for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit,' belong beside it and not against it. One speaks of what the people are called to do, the other of what only God can do, and the Bible allows both to stand.

The passage should also be read with care about the land. The promise to give back the land of Israel was spoken to exiles who were about to wait decades for its first stage, and its application to any later political situation is argued by Christians in different ways. The New Testament takes the heart of the promise, a people with a changed heart and God's own presence, as the thing that now reaches all nations.

debates.question: How should Ezekiel 11:3 be read: 'Is not the time near to build houses?'

views.label: A boast of coming prosperity
views.case: The BSB reads the Hebrew as a question expecting yes: the time is near to build houses. The leaders are confident that, with the exiles gone, rebuilding and settling are about to begin, and the city will be the safe pot that keeps them as choice meat. Ezekiel 24:3 to 5 uses the pot with the opposite sense for the same period, so the leaders are claiming a safety that the prophet has already denied.

views.label: A denial that disaster is near
views.case: Older English versions, such as the King James, read it as a statement that the time is not near, so let us build houses. The Hebrew is compact and can be taken either way. On this reading the leaders are saying that the warnings of Jeremiah and Ezekiel are a long way off, and life can go on, which fits the proverb answered in 12:22 and 12:27.

views.label: A mockery of the exiles' letter
views.case: Jeremiah had told the exiles to build houses in Babylon, Jeremiah 29:5, and the leaders may be turning the phrase against them, as if to say that the exiles are the ones who should settle while the city's people hold the real centre.

debates.bearing: All three readings leave the point intact. The leaders have decided that they are safe, and God's reply in 11:7 turns the picture around. The translation question is a real one, but the verdict does not depend on it.

debates.question: Is 11:16 a 'little sanctuary' or a sanctuary 'for a little while'?

views.label: A little sanctuary
views.case: The Hebrew word me'at means small or few, and some Jewish tradition took the phrase to mean a minor sanctuary, which later readers connected with the gathering places of the Jews in exile. The idea is that God Himself would be the sanctuary, wherever the exiles gathered.

views.label: A sanctuary for a little while
views.case: The same word is often used of a short time. The BSB reads it this way, and the sense would be that God has been a sanctuary to the exiles for the present period, until the return promised in 11:17. This fits the context of a temporary scattering.

views.label: Both senses are meant
views.case: A word that can carry both size and time suits a statement whose point is that God's presence is not tied to a large building or a long season. His nearness to the exiles is real but humble, and it is enough for the time.

debates.bearing: Either way, the verse tells the exiles that the sanctuary they had lost was not the whole of God's presence. This truth is taken up by Jesus when He says that where two or three gather in His name, He is there, Matthew 18:20.

debates.question: When is the promise of 11:17 to 20 fulfilled?

views.label: In the return from Babylon
views.case: The gathering and the return of the land began under Cyrus, and the restoration of the temple followed. Some readers see in this the immediate fulfilment of the promise, with the new heart as a reforming of the community after the exile.

views.label: In Christ and the church
views.case: The New Testament says that the new covenant promises are fulfilled through the blood of Jesus and the gift of the Spirit, Luke 22:20, 2 Corinthians 3:3 and Hebrews 8. The post-exilic community did not receive a new heart in the way the prophets describe, so the fulfilment is in the new birth of believers from every nation.

views.label: In Christ, with a future for Israel and the land
views.case: Others hold that the promise is fulfilled in Christ and that it also awaits a future gathering of Israel to the land, as Romans 11 and Ezekiel 37 are sometimes read. The land and the heart are seen as parts of one promise.

debates.bearing: All agree that the heart of the promise, God's own Spirit in His people, has come in Christ. The disagreement concerns the land and Israel's future, and it should be held with humility, since the text of Ezekiel itself places the gift of the heart first.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter turns on a handful of Hebrew words that are easier to see than to translate.

The first is basar, flesh or meat. In 11:3 the leaders say the city is the pot and they are the basar, the choice cut kept safe by the walls of a cooking vessel. In 11:7 God reverses it, and the meat becomes the slain they have laid in the city. Then in 11:19 the same word returns in the phrase heart of flesh. What a boast of security had made of the word, the promise now remakes. The heart of stone, lev ha'even, is a heart like a rock, hard and unyielding, and flesh here is its opposite, a heart that can feel and bend.

The second is the contrast between gift and command. Ezekiel 11:19 and 36:26 say that God will give a new heart and put a new spirit within them. Yet Ezekiel 18:31 commands the same people to fashion for themselves a new heart and a new spirit. The same pair of nouns stands in both places, and the book does not resolve the tension by explanation. It sets the call to repent and the promise of re-creation next to each other, as the New Testament does with the call to work out salvation and the statement that God is at work in us, Philippians 2:12 and 13.

The third is the phrase usually translated singleness of heart, which is literally one heart, lev echad. Jeremiah 32:39 has 'one heart and one way,' and the sense is of a heart no longer divided between the LORD and the idols, a division the prophets repeatedly describe. The 'new spirit' is in the Hebrew a new ruach, and the word that means spirit also means wind and breath. The idea of a new breath within lies behind the vision of dry bones in 37:14, 'I will put My Spirit in you and you will live.' The preposition for 'within' is the word for the middle or inside, and the gift is therefore one that works from the center.

A fourth item is the purpose clause that follows in 11:20, so that they may walk in My statutes and keep My ordinances. The people had failed at exactly that, 11:12, and the new heart is given so that the failure is undone. The two words, statutes and ordinances, are the standard pair for the whole of the law. Following that is the covenant formula, 'they will be My people, and I will be their God,' which is the oldest summary of the relationship, here placed at the end of the promise as its goal.

A fifth detail is in the names. Pelatiah's name has the root of escape or deliverance, and he dies while the prophet is speaking. Whether or not the name was heard as an irony, the story makes the death a sign that the word is no empty one, and it is that death which draws out the cry of 11:13. Lastly, the footnote tells us that 'Chaldea' in 11:24 can also be read as Babylonia, the land of the exiles, where the vision ends and where the word is to be spoken.

typology.type: A sanctuary among the scattered, Ezekiel 11:16
typology.fulfillment: God declares Himself a sanctuary to people far from the temple. Isaiah had said that the LORD would be 'a sanctuary' to some and a stone of stumbling to others, Isaiah 8:14. The Gospel of John says the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and Jesus calls His own body the temple, John 2:19 to 21. For those who were far off, Paul says, Christ has made peace and given access to the Father, Ephesians 2:13 to 18. The correspondence is of presence with those who have no building. The escalation is that the sanctuary is now a person who has Himself been cast out. It falls short only in that Ezekiel's sanctuary was provisional, while Christ's presence is permanent.

typology.type: The heart of stone exchanged for a heart of flesh, Ezekiel 11:19
typology.fulfillment: The surgery of the heart that Moses promised, Deuteronomy 30:6, and Ezekiel and Jeremiah describe, Jeremiah 31:33, is carried out through the Spirit. Paul says believers are a letter written on 'tablets of human hearts,' 2 Corinthians 3:3, and that the Spirit gives life where the letter kills, 2 Corinthians 3:6. Jesus speaks of being born of water and the Spirit, John 3:5. The correspondence is of a transformed inner life. The type is not yet complete, since believers still struggle with the flesh, Romans 7, and the final renewal of the heart waits for the resurrection.

typology.type: The gathering of the scattered, Ezekiel 11:17
typology.fulfillment: God promises to gather His people from the countries to which they have been scattered. The shepherd of Ezekiel 34:12 and 13 does the same thing. John says that Jesus died for the nation, and also for the scattered children of God, to gather them together into one, John 11:51 and 52. Jesus Himself longed to gather the children of Jerusalem like a hen gathers her chicks, Matthew 23:37. The correspondence is of a people called back together by God. The escalation is that the gathering is not limited to those of one ancestry but extends to every nation. It falls short only in that the full gathering is still to come, Revelation 7:9.

typology.type: The glory standing over the mountain on the east, Ezekiel 11:23
typology.fulfillment: The glory pauses over the mountain east of the city, which is the Mount of Olives, and it does not return in this vision. Jesus goes up from that same mountain, Acts 1:9 to 12, and the angels say He will return in the same way. Zechariah 14:4 places His feet on it. The correspondence is of a place of waiting between departure and return. The type is of a presence that withdraws only in order to come again, and in Christ the glory is both ascended and promised.

study.christ:
The chapter points to Christ most clearly through its promise, and the promise comes in three parts: a sanctuary for the exiled, a Spirit for the stony-hearted, and a gathering for the scattered. Each part is taken up in the New Testament and tied to Him.

The sanctuary comes first. In 11:16 God says that He has been a sanctuary to those far from Jerusalem. The leaders in the city had said the exiles were far from the LORD, and God answers that He is nearer to them than the temple is to those who defile it. It is Jesus who makes this concrete. He says of Himself that He is the temple that will be destroyed and raised, John 2:19 to 21, and promises that where two or three gather in His name He is there, Matthew 18:20. People who thought they were outside, the poor, the sick, the foreigners, found the presence of God in Him. Isaiah had said that the LORD would be 'a sanctuary' and also a stone that makes people stumble, Isaiah 8:14, and the two sides are exactly what Jesus' ministry produced.

The Spirit is the second. 'I will give them singleness of heart and put a new spirit within them,' 11:19, is the promise that Christ fulfills by sending the Holy Spirit after His exaltation, Acts 2:33. At the Last Supper He says the cup is the new covenant in His blood, Luke 22:20. The writer of Hebrews says that He is the mediator of a better covenant, and quotes Jeremiah's promise that God will write His laws on their hearts, Hebrews 8:6 to 10. Paul adds that what the law could not do because of the flesh, God did by sending His Son, so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit, Romans 8:3 and 4. The stone heart is not made soft by effort but by the Spirit that Christ gives, and this is why believers can be told that they now have 'one heart and soul,' Acts 4:32.

The gathering is the third. Caiaphas, without knowing it, said that Jesus would die for the nation and also for the scattered children of God, to gather them into one, John 11:51 and 52. The promise of 11:17 is not only fulfilled in a return to the land. It is fulfilled in the cross, which brings people from every nation to belong to one people.

There is a sobering side. The glory of the LORD, in this chapter, rises from the city and stands on the east. Jesus, in the days before the cross, weeps over the city and says its house is left desolate, Luke 19:41 to 44 and Matthew 23:38. He leaves from the Mount of Olives, Acts 1:9 to 12. In Him the whole pattern of departure and promise is acted out once more.

The interpretation needs one caution. The leaders of Jerusalem in this chapter are not a code for the Jewish people of Jesus' day, and the exiles are not a code for the church. The chapter is about a particular conflict among Judeans in the sixth century before Christ, and it points to Him by the promise that He fulfills, not by a hidden scheme.
study.god:
Ezekiel 11 presents a God who knows, who judges, and who gives, and it shows how these belong together.

He knows the mind. 'I know the thoughts that arise in your minds,' He says in 11:5, and the sentence follows an account of the plot that the men were making. The God who is the Lord of the temple is also the Lord of what is said in the gate of the city and thought in private. The people of chapter 8 had said that the LORD does not see; here the answer is that He sees what is spoken and what is thought. Jeremiah asks, 'Do I not fill the heavens and the earth?' Jeremiah 23:24, and the psalmist asks where he could flee from God's presence, Psalm 139:7.

He judges with a moral purpose. The charge against the leaders is specific: they have multiplied the slain in the city, 11:6, and they have conformed to the ordinances of the nations instead of walking in God's own, 11:12. The judgment fits the crime. They feared the sword, and the sword will come, 11:8. They thought they would be kept safe in the city, and they will be brought out of it. The repeated refrain, 'Then you will know that I am the LORD,' 11:10 and 11:12, is not a mere description of what they will learn. It is what the judgment is for, the vindication of the God they ignored.

He is present with the displaced. The God of Israel who is said to be enthroned between the cherubim declares that He is a sanctuary for the exiles, 11:16. God is not tied to Jerusalem, and His mercy is not tied to merit. It is just here that He chooses to be near. Isaiah 57:15 says that the high and holy One lives with the contrite and lowly, and this chapter shows the principle in a historical case.

He is the giver of the heart. The promise of 11:19 and 11:20 is that God will do the very thing the commandment required. The people will walk in His statutes because He has changed them. Salvation is not mainly a matter of human resolve but of divine re-creation, a conclusion Paul draws when he says that God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, Romans 5:5. The Spirit's role is also worth observing. In this chapter, the Spirit lifts the prophet, falls on him, speaks through him and carries him, 11:1, 11:5 and 11:24, and then He is promised to the people as the gift that changes them. God's saving work is by His Spirit from first to last.

He is faithful to a covenant that the people have broken. 'They will be My people, and I will be their God,' 11:20, is a formula older than the monarchy and unbroken by the exile. The God who judges is the same God who has not given up His purposes.

For worship, the chapter suggests humility and thanks. We are not the guardians of God's presence, and we cannot keep ourselves in it. It is a gift to the scattered, who find that God has been a sanctuary where they thought He was absent, and a gift that goes with a transformed heart.

crossReferences.note: Jeremiah's vision of two baskets of figs calls the exiles to Babylon the good figs, and promises to build them up, bring them back and give them a heart to know the LORD. It is the same verdict as Ezekiel 11:16 to 20, spoken from Jerusalem, and it stands against the leaders' boast that the exiles were far from God.

Jeremiah's letter tells the exiles to build houses, plant gardens and seek the welfare of Babylon. The leaders' phrase about building houses in Ezekiel 11:3 may be a rival or mocking echo of this advice, and it shows that the real conflict was about which group God was going to bless.

The parable of the cooking pot at the siege, where the city is the pot filled with the choice pieces and left to boil. Ezekiel 11 uses the same image from the other side, in which the leaders try to claim the pot as their protection and God turns it into the place where the slain lie.

The fullest statement of the promise in 11:17 to 20. It adds that God will sprinkle clean water on them, cleanse them from their idols, and put His Spirit within them to cause them to walk in His statutes. This is the passage Jesus has in mind when He speaks to Nicodemus of water and the Spirit.

The new covenant, in which God puts His law in their minds and writes it on their hearts. Jeremiah and Ezekiel were contemporaries and speak of the same hope in different words, and Hebrews 8 quotes Jeremiah to show that the hope has been fulfilled.

Moses promises that the LORD Himself will circumcise the hearts of the people and their descendants, so that they will love Him with all their heart. Ezekiel's new heart is the same gift, spoken to a generation in exile, and it shows the promise was part of the Torah's own hope.

The prophet commands the house of Israel to fashion for themselves a new heart and a new spirit. Set against 11:19, it shows that the book holds the call to repent and the promise that God will give a new heart together, and that the second is the ground of the first.

After the fall, the survivors in the ruins say that Abraham was one man and had the land, so surely it is given to them. It is a later form of the claim in 11:15 that the land belongs to those who stayed, and it shows that the attitude outlasted the first warning.

Paul says the Corinthians are a letter from Christ, written with the Spirit of the living God on tablets of human hearts. He is describing the fulfilment of Ezekiel's promise of a heart of flesh, and shows that the change of heart is the work of the Spirit through the gospel.

Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one can see the kingdom without being born again, of water and the Spirit, and is surprised that a teacher of Israel does not understand. The sources of his surprise are the promises of Ezekiel 11 and 36, which any serious student of the prophets should have known.

The glory that stood over the mountain on the east in 11:23 comes back from the east in 43:1 to 5 and fills the temple. The departure in this chapter is therefore not an end, and the two scenes are meant to frame the whole book.

study.oneStory:
Behind Ezekiel 11 lies the question that every exile story asks: if God gave the land, the temple and the king, what does it mean that they are gone? The Bible's first answer is in Genesis 3, where the people were driven east from the garden. The prophets repeat it. The nation that was given a new Eden in the land of promise, a place where God's presence lived among them, has repeated the old failure and is going out again.

This chapter's contribution is to put the hope in the same breath as the verdict. It says that the problem is not only the land or the temple but the heart. Moses had said in Deuteronomy 29 and 30 that a people who could not keep the covenant would need God Himself to circumcise their hearts, and the history of Israel under the kings confirmed it. Jeremiah's saying that the heart is deceitful above all things, Jeremiah 17:9, and his picture of sin engraved with an iron stylus on the tablets of the heart, Jeremiah 17:1, describe what Ezekiel 11:19 means by a heart of stone. The only thing that could change it was a gift, and the gift is promised here.

The New Testament shows the gift arriving. At the Last Supper Jesus says that His blood is the blood of the new covenant, Luke 22:20. At Pentecost the Spirit is poured out, Acts 2:1 to 4, and Peter says that Jesus has received the promised Holy Spirit from the Father and has poured it out, Acts 2:33. The hearts that were stone become living. Paul says that believers are a letter written on tablets of human hearts, 2 Corinthians 3:3, and that the people of God are now from every nation, so that the gathering of Ezekiel 11:17 becomes the gathering of a worldwide church, John 11:52.

The story is not complete. Creation still groans and believers still struggle with sin. But the end is already clear. In Revelation the dwelling place of God is with man, and the covenant formula that Ezekiel quotes, 'they will be My people, and I will be their God,' is spoken over the whole of redeemed humanity, Revelation 21:3. The stone heart is gone, the glory is back, and there is no longer an east gate to leave by. The God who was a little sanctuary for people scattered in a foreign land becomes the sanctuary of the whole new creation, Revelation 21:22.

sermon.title: Does God Ever Give Up on People? (Ezek. 10-11)
sermon.why: Carson traces both the judgment on Jerusalem's wicked counselors and the astonishing promise of a new heart and new spirit within chapter 11, showing how the exile's darkest moment carries within it the seed of God's greatest covenant hope, exactly the tension this study is built around.

quiz.q: What false confidence do the twenty-five leaders express with the image of the pot and the meat?

options.text: That Jerusalem's walls make its inhabitants safe like meat protected in a cooking pot, while plotting violence and killing.
options.note: Verses 3, 6-7 show this image expressed pride in the city's supposed safety even while filling it with the slain.

options.text: That Jerusalem's food supply would never run low.
options.note: The imagery is about false security, not literal food supply.

options.text: That the exiles would soon return and rebuild the city together.
options.note: The leaders are dismissive of the exiles, not planning a reunion with them.

options.text: That Ezekiel himself was the source of the city's danger.
options.note: The danger comes from the leaders' own wicked counsel and violence, not from Ezekiel.

quiz.q: What does God promise to be for the exiles while they are scattered among the nations?

options.text: A sanctuary in small measure, His presence remaining with them even away from the ruined temple.
options.note: Verse 16 makes this explicit promise of God's nearness in exile.

options.text: Complete silence and absence until they physically return to the land.
options.note: The text promises the opposite: God's presence with them during the exile itself.

options.text: A replacement temple built by their own hands in Babylon.
options.note: No physical temple is built; the sanctuary described is God's own presence, not a structure.

options.text: A temporary curse with no promise of restoration.
options.note: The passage promises far more than mere endurance; it promises gathering and transformation.

quiz.q: What does God promise to give His people in verse 19?

options.text: Singleness of heart and a new spirit, removing a heart of stone and giving a heart of flesh.
options.note: Verse 19 states this transformation explicitly and directly.

options.text: A new set of written laws to replace the old ones.
options.note: The promise is an inward transformation of the heart, not a replacement legal code.

options.text: Wealth and prosperity as a reward for enduring exile.
options.note: The promise concerns inward transformation, not material reward.

options.text: A new set of priests to replace the corrupt ones in Jerusalem.
options.note: The passage addresses the people's hearts broadly, not specifically a reformed priesthood.

quiz.q: What happens to Pelatiah while Ezekiel is prophesying?

options.text: He dies suddenly, prompting Ezekiel to cry out in fear for the remnant of Israel.
options.note: Verse 13 records his death and Ezekiel's anguished cry in response.

options.text: He repents publicly and leads the other counselors to repentance.
options.note: The text records his death, not a scene of repentance.

options.text: He is taken into exile alongside Ezekiel's audience.
options.note: He dies in Jerusalem; he is not exiled.

options.text: He is promoted to a position of greater authority.
options.note: His death, not promotion, is what the text records.

quiz.q: Where does the glory of the LORD finally come to rest at the end of this chapter?

options.text: Above the mountain east of the city.
options.note: Verse 23 states the glory rose from within the city and stood over the mountain east of it.

options.text: It returns permanently to the Most Holy Place.
options.note: The chapter records continued departure, not a return to the temple's inner room.

options.text: It disappears entirely with no further mention in the book.
options.note: Ezekiel 43 later promises and records the glory's future return.

options.text: It remains at the east gate of the temple itself.
options.note: By this chapter's end the glory has moved further, to the mountain east of the city.

questions: The Jerusalem leaders felt falsely secure, treating the city like a pot that could protect them regardless of their violence and injustice. Where might you be trusting in circumstances or status rather than a right relationship with God?

Those in exile were despised by those still in the city, yet it was the exiles God promised to restore. Who do you tend to write off as 'far from the LORD', and how does this passage challenge that judgment?

God promises a new heart and new spirit that enables obedience from within rather than mere outward compliance. Where in your life are you relying on willpower rather than the Spirit's transforming work?
Ezekiel cried out in anguish when he saw judgment fall, even on a wicked man. How do you hold together grief over sin's consequences with confidence in God's ultimate promise of restoration?

God calls Himself a 'sanctuary in small measure' to His exiled people, present with them even far from the temple. Where do you need to remember that God's presence is not confined to a building, a routine, or a season of ease?

translationNotes.note: The proverb 'the city is the cooking pot, and we are the meat' likely expressed a boast of protected privilege; God ironically reverses its meaning in verse 7, applying it instead to the slain the leaders themselves have filled the city with.

The BSB smooths an appositional phrase describing the exiles as 'your brothers, your relatives, your fellow exiles, and the whole house of Israel', emphasizing the totality of those Jerusalem's residents had written off.

Some manuscripts and versions read 'one heart' rather than 'a new heart', both conveying the same basic promise of undivided, transformed devotion; the BSB's 'singleness of heart' captures the sense of a heart no longer split between the LORD and idols.
